maximum_defensible_wording: In a preregistered clean-room reproduction on SPIDER's Graph fragment store (12 fragments, 3 sandbox sites, scripted policies, lexical-hash embedder, deterministic summarizer), SGDR-style stepwise retrieval scored by alpha*cos(task, desc) + (1-alpha)*cos(current-state summary, desc) with pool top-M=max(3k,20) and greedy MMR (lambda=0.7) retrieved executable-correct fragments strictly more often than task-text-only retrieval with identical reranking machinery under paraphrased goals and shifted entry contexts (36/74 vs 25/74 correct@1; 11 paired wins, 0 reversals). Auditor-side controls show the gain requires the correct current-state summary: fusing a wrong-context summary or using a summary-only score falls back to baseline level (both 24/74). Under identical execution policies the advantage converted into fewer novel exploration actions than task-only retrieval on both goal regimes (39 vs 42 literal; 36 vs 42 paraphrase) with equal-or-higher subgoal success (.90/.90 vs .90/.80). The retrieval-level advantage is concentrated in one site's dynamic-content menu-disambiguation cluster (int.dyn.nav/ex2/start; 8/2/1 wins); no advantage over task-only retrieval was observed for login/pager addressing. Relative to hand-authored exact goal_sig addressing, the mechanism wins only in the natural-language-consumer regime; when signatures exist, exact addressing remains more action-efficient (21 vs 39 novel on the literal slice). Evidence tier: PROOF OF CONCEPT. Not established: WebArena-scale effects, neural embedders, LLM summarizers, larger libraries, cross-site/cross-domain transfer, robustness of constant-text fusion controls under hashed embeddings.
